metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the subject's choice matches the deterministic prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. Because the trials are specifically designed to pit the highest available validity cue against the sum of the remaining lower-validity cues, TTB and WADD make consistently opposing predictions on most trials. Data generated by TTB will show a very high match rate (close to 1.0, minus lapse noise), whereas data generated by WADD will show a significantly lower match rate, as WADD integrates the compensatory evidence from the lesser cues.

By design, the first discriminating cue always favors Option A across all trials, meaning Take The Best (TTB) will consistently choose Option A (response = 0). However, in trials where Option B has a greater number of positive features than Option A (i.e., sum(B) > sum(A)), the compensatory nature of the Weighted Additive model (WADD) leads it to favor Option B, because the sum of the lower-validity cues outweighs the single highest-validity cue. This metric calculates the proportion of times Option B is chosen on exactly these trials. TTB predicts a value near 0 (driven only by noise), while WADD predicts a high value (often > 0.5).

In Trial 3, both Option A and Option B have exactly one positive feature. The Tallying model evaluates this as a perfect tie (1 vs 1) and will predict a 50% chance of choosing A for every subject, with any deviation from 0.5 being purely due to binomial sampling noise. WADD, however, assigns subjective weights to the specific features present. Because these weights vary and are unlikely to be perfectly equal, WADD will systematically prefer one option over the other for any given subject. By calculating the mean per-subject absolute deviation from a 0.5 choice proportion on this trial, we expect a value close to 0 (specifically, the expected absolute deviation of a Binomial(16, 0.5)/16) for Tallying, and a significantly larger value for WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chose the option [0, 0, 1, 1, 1] over the option [1, 1, 0, 0, 0]. Under the Weighted Additive (WADD) model with validities [0.9, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5, 0.5], both options have exactly the same weighted sum (1.6), so WADD predicts subjects will guess (a choice proportion of 0.5). Under the Tallying (Equal Weight) model, the option [0, 0, 1, 1, 1] has a higher sum (3 vs 2), so Tallying predicts it will be chosen consistently above chance. By focusing exclusively on these perfectly balanced trials, we can maximally discriminate between the two decision rules.

To robustly isolate the validity bias from the dominant tallying heuristic, this metric computes the within-subject residual choice probability after controlling for the exact tally difference. For every subject and every tally difference level, we compute their empirical mean probability of choosing Option B. We then subtract this mean from their actual trial-by-trial choices to get a 'residual choice'. Under Pure Tallying, this residual is pure noise and is strictly uncorrelated with the difference in cue validities between the options. Under Tallying with Validity Bias, this residual will be positively correlated with the validity difference. By computing the covariance between the residual choice and the exact validity difference (using the true experimental validities) across all trials, we perfectly partial out the tallying effect, yielding an expected value of exactly 0 for Pure Tallying and a robustly positive value for the Competing Theory. This approach optimally weights all 96 trials, minimizing binomial noise and maximizing the signal-to-noise ratio.

This metric calculates the proportion of times a subject chooses the option with the higher validity score, strictly on trials where the simple tally of positive features is tied. The pure Tallying model predicts random guessing (0.5) on these trials because the tally counts are equal. In contrast, the Tallying with Validity Bias model predicts a systematic preference (>0.5) for the option that possesses the higher-validity features. Isolating tie trials provides a clean, highly discriminatory test between the two theories.
